$AAPL Apple shares are down nearly 4% in premarket trading after being roughly flat going into last night’s earnings call. What happened?

Apple doesn’t put guidance in its release, but on the call it guided to December-quarter revenue growth of 7% to 10%, above the 5.9% FactSet consensus, even as Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan expects memory-related supply constraints on Mac and iPad.

So far so good. But CFO Kevan Parekh then guided gross margin to 45% to 46%, citing higher memory costs and the Siri AI ramp. That’s below the 47% analysts expected, according to Bloomberg, and down from 47.9% in the fiscal fourth quarter. Relatedly he also expects higher margin Services growth to slow to 8% to 9%, short of the 10% analysts expected.

That matters at Apple’s valuation: the stock trades at 36 times next year’s expected earnings, with earnings growth of only 1% expected, per Oppenheimer’s Martin Yang in The Wall Street Journal. By my math, each point of gross margin on the guided revenue midpoint is worth about $0.09 a share in the December quarter, so falling 1 to 2 points short of the 47% estimate costs roughly $0.09 to $0.18 in EPS.

https://t.co/NdwHHVtmGQ

Yardeni says "a blue wave could deliver a cold shoulder for stocks," but if so buy the dip: 

Wall Street traditionally welcomes political gridlock because it reduces the likelihood that Congress will pass extremist legislation. But this time could be different for two reasons.

First, deepening partisanship could turn gridlock into damaging political paralysis at a time when the Bond Vigilantes are already uneasy about Washington's unsustainable fiscal trajectory. A Democratic sweep could complicate negotiations over government spending and the debt ceiling. Prolonged shutdowns and fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher, weighing on equity valuations.

Second, gridlock's traditional ability to constrain policymaking may not hold this time. President Donald Trump has relied heavily on executive authority... A Democratic-controlled Congress may therefore do little to restrain him. Moreover, with the midterms behind him, Trump may feel even less constrained politically and more willing to pursue controversial policies through executive action. 

Hence, a blue wave could deliver a cold shower for stocks, though we would view a significant selloff as a buying opportunity given the remarkable strength of the economy and corporate earnings.

Some caution on the post-midterm rally everyone is expecting is appropriate. 

Based on Truist’s composite chart of midterm seasonality since 1950, the S&P 500 is normally up only about 1% at the end of October, finishing up about 5%, with roughly 3 points of that coming after Election Day (which falls between November 2nd and 8th). 

This year, though, the S&P 500 was already up 10.7% through October.

Elections, JOLTS, and ADP Highlight Tuesday's Calendar

It's Election Day, with Americans voting in the midterm elections (all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships are on the ballot).

In US economic data, Tuesday brings us September JOLTS job openings and factory orders (which include final durable goods), and October vehicle sales.

There are no Fed speakers scheduled, although the Global Research Forum on International Macroeconomics and Finance, organized by the Fed, ECB and New York Fed, begins in Washington (through November 4), so there may very well be media interviews.

There are no non-Bill (>1yr in maturity) US Treasury auctions this week.

37 S&P 500 components report, seven of them with market caps over $100bn:

After the close: AMD ($AMD), Amgen ($AMGN), Arista Networks ($ANET), Booking Holdings ($BKNG), Block ($XYZ), AIG ($AIG), Prudential Financial ($PRU), International Flavors & Fragrances ($IFF), Super Micro Computer ($SMCI), Skyworks Solutions ($SWKS), Assurant ($AIZ), Jack Henry & Associates ($JKHY) and Mosaic ($MOS)

Before the open: Pfizer ($PFE), Eaton ($ETN), Marathon Petroleum ($MPC), Apollo Global Management ($APO), Ametek ($AME), Keurig Dr Pepper ($KDP), Waters ($WAT), Yum! Brands ($YUM), Sysco ($SYY), Archer-Daniels-Midland ($ADM), Fiserv ($FISV), Expeditors International ($EXPD), Broadridge Financial ($BR), Fidelity National Information Services ($FIS), DuPont ($DD), Leidos ($LDOS), Ball ($BALL), Revvity ($RVTY), Zebra Technologies ($ZBRA), Gartner ($IT), Pinnacle West ($PNW), Henry Schein ($HSIC) and Aptiv ($APTV)

Time not announced: Bio-Techne ($TECH)

Outside the S&P 500, Shopify ($SHOP), Energy Transfer ($ET), Ferrari ($RACE), Bayer ($BAYRY) and Intesa Sanpaolo ($ISNPY) report.

Ex-US highlights include the Reserve Bank of Australia's decision (10:30pm ET Monday; Deutsche Bank expects a hold), October CPI from Switzerland, South Korea and Turkey (plus Turkey PPI), New Zealand's Q3 labor force survey, Japan's October monetary base and France's September budget balance. ECB Governing Council members Kocher, Dolenc, Radev, Escriva, Moulin, Nagel and Sleijpen speak, as do the Bank of Canada's Macklem and Rogers, and UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Healey takes oral questions in the House of Commons.

Japanese markets are closed for Culture Day.

It sort of passed under the radar, but last week after 13 years the Bank of Japan says underlying inflation has finally reached its 2% target, the goal it set in January 2013 and once expected to hit in about two years. Still, the BOJ held at 1.25% on an 8-1 vote, with only hawk Takata dissenting for a hike, and Governor Ueda kept December firmly in play.

The new Outlook Report leans hawkish:
▪️ Core CPI forecast (ex-fresh food) for fiscal 2027 raised to 2.6% from 2.4%; fiscal 2026 unchanged at 2.5%
▪️ Ex-fresh food and energy peaks at 2.7% in fiscal 2027
▪️ Risks to prices judged skewed to the upside
▪️ Growth stuck around 0.7% a year
▪️ ETF sales nearly triple to about ¥860 billion a year, cutting the unwind to 43 years from 110+

The hold was even as the BOJ is still deeply accommodative. At 1.25%, the policy rate is about -1.35% in real terms against Tokyo’s 2.6% core reading.

 Bloomberg Economics sees hikes in December, March and July to 2%, the top of ING’s 1.75% to 2.00% neutral range. Even then, the real rate would be about -0.6% against the board’s own fiscal 2027 forecast.

For the yen, the Fed-BOJ gap is roughly half its mid-2024 level, yet the yen is only about 3% off its weakest levels. If both the Fed and the BOJ hike in December, the gap doesn’t narrow, which fits ING’s call for a 155 to 160 range.

AI infrastructure spending is driving a sharp increase in US bank lending:

Commercial and Industrial (C&I) loans at large US banks surged +11.4% YoY in October, to $1.6 trillion, the most since June 2020.

This also marked their largest YoY growth since February 2023.

In Q3, C&I loans at the 25 largest US banks grew almost +10.0% YoY, the strongest growth in 10 years excluding pandemic-related swings.

This represents a sharp reversal from an -8.0% YoY contraction in Q4 2025.

The surge has been driven by rising borrowing demand from Big Tech companies and data-center developers to fund AI infrastructure projects.

At the same time, regional lenders are providing credit to construction companies and other businesses benefiting from the investment boom.

The data-center buildout is increasingly being funded by debt.

⚡With Election Day upon us, we've expanded the prediction market dashboard: every competitive Senate race, 40+ House seats and the key governor contests, all live on @Kalshi pricing. We'll keep adding races through the day and into election night as new ones come into play.

A few things the last month of data shows:

• Democrats Sweep (House + Senate) is up 10 points in five days to 75%
• Kansas Senate: Hamilton (D) now 63%, up from a one-month low of 27%, the biggest move on the board
• Iowa Senate flipped this weekend, Turek (D) now 52%
• Maine: Jackson (D) +11 on the week vs. Collins
• PA-01: Harvie (D) 65%, up from 35% a month ago against Fitzpatrick
• KY-06, MT-01 and NC-01 have all more than doubled from their one-month lows
• Governors: Georgia, Nevada, Ohio and Texas each moved 20+ toward Democrats in 30 days

The only notable move the other way: NY-17, where Lawler (R) picked up 5 today.

First polls close tomorrow at 6pm ET in Kentucky's 6th. We'll be watching it with you.

tweets.text: Bitcoin needs to hold the low $70,000 levels for the market regime to remain bullish. Crypto breadth, which posted its strongest, most sustained outperformance in over a year, has collapsed. Washed-out levels but bitcoin:native support needs to hold. Liquidity is tighter than what the markets are comfortable with. Several years of Growth in Debt > liquidity, and this is the inevitable outcome. The response is also inevitable, although the mechanism of action is more dynamic and unclear this time round --> Fed kneecapped, Treasury numero uno. So expect a combo of actions; TGA drawdown, buybacks, increasing short-end issuance, even potentially gold revaluation. Next 3-6 months will be wild.
